messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Chaplain
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 77

**Clinical Vignette: Mr. L.**

Mr. L. is a 34-year-old South Eastern Asian man, a widower, who presents as thoughtful and measured, though his hands tremble slightly when he describes the events of the past year. He works as a chaplain at a large urban hospital, a role he has held for nearly a decade. He sought therapy after a colleague noticed he was avoiding the hospital’s main entrance and taking three flights of stairs to reach the oncology unit, even when his knees ached.

The traumatic event occurred fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Mr. L. had just finished a twelve-hour shift. He was walking to his car in the hospital’s designated staff parking lot, a route he had taken without incident for years. He was tired, thinking about a young mother he had sat with who had just received a terminal diagnosis. He did not see the two men until they were already on him. One pressed a cold, hard object—he believes it was a gun—against the back of his neck. The other demanded his wallet and phone. Mr. L. complied immediately, speaking in a low, steady voice he recognized from a thousand bedside prayers. He told them, “It’s okay. Take it. Just don’t hurt me.” They took his belongings and ran. The entire interaction lasted perhaps forty-five seconds. No one was physically injured.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. L. told himself he was fine. He had counseled countless victims of violence; he knew the statistics, the coping skills. He repeated to himself, “It was just a robbery. I wasn’t hurt. I am blessed.” He refused to file a police report, telling his supervisor it was a waste of resources. But internally, something had shifted. He began to feel a constant, low-grade static in his chest. He stopped walking to his car after dark, asking security for an escort. Then he stopped walking to his car at all, instead taking the bus and getting off two stops early so he could approach the hospital from a different direction. He began to avoid the staff parking lot entirely, a place he had once considered a safe, mundane part of his day.

The avoidance has since metastasized. He no longer goes to the grocery store after 5 p.m. He will not stand in line at a bank. He scans every room he enters for exits, a habit he finds exhausting. The worst moments come when he is ministering to a patient. Last month, while praying with a man dying of heart failure, the patient’s hand suddenly gripped his wrist. The sensation—the sudden, unexpected pressure—sent a jolt through Mr. L.’s body. He saw the parking lot. He felt the cold metal. He pulled his hand away and left the room mid-prayer, apologizing to the empty hallway. He now conducts his bedside visits with his hands clasped firmly behind his back, a posture his patients sometimes misinterpret as aloofness.

He has nightmares, but not of the mugging itself. He dreams of his late wife, who died of cancer five years ago. In the dreams, she is alive, but she is always standing in the parking lot, looking at him with a sad, knowing expression. He tries to reach her, but his legs will not move. He wakes in a cold sweat, convinced for a moment that he is back on that asphalt, that the gun is still there. He then lies awake, running through the night of her death, wondering if he did enough, said enough. The mugging seems to have pried open a door to an older grief he thought he had sealed shut.

At work, his colleagues notice he is quieter. He used to be known for his gentle humor in the staff break room; now he eats lunch alone in his office, with the door closed and his back to the wall. He tells himself he is just being more professional, more focused. But he knows the truth: the world, once a place he navigated with faith and a sense of purpose, now feels like a series of ambushes waiting to happen. He feels untethered, a shepherd who has lost his own sense of safety.
